description: The fundamental condition where available resources are insufficient to satisfy all human wants.
The act of selecting among alternatives due to the existence of scarcity.
The alternatives that must be given up when a decision is made to pursue a specific action.
The value of the next best alternative forgone as the result of making a decision.
The subjective value or benefit gained from consuming or acquiring one additional unit of a good or service.
The examination of the additional benefits of an activity compared to the additional costs incurred.
Factors, such as financial rewards or penalties, that motivate individuals to behave in certain ways.
The continuous process by which individuals alter their plans in response to the changing actions of others within a market.
The process by which individuals work together, often mediated by institutions or markets, to achieve mutually beneficial ends.
The structures and institutions through which societies organize the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services.
Information passed between economic actors that indicates underlying market conditions, such as relative scarcity.
The legally or socially recognized authority to determine how a resource or asset is used and to retain the benefits it generates.
The state of having exclusive rights and control over property or an asset.
The act of trading goods or services between parties without coercion, occurring when both expect to gain.
The practice of forcing another party to act in an involuntary manner through threats or intimidation, contrary to voluntary exchange.
The process of convincing another party to change their beliefs, preferences, or actions through reasoning or appeal rather than force.
A social order characterized by an extensive division of labor, private property, and reliance on voluntary exchange.
The subjective importance, usefulness, or worth placed on a good or service by an individual.
The accumulation of valuable economic resources that can be measured in terms of either real goods or money value.
The process of producing goods or services that satisfy consumer desires, thus increasing the total value within society.
The mutual transfer of goods, services, or ideas between two or more economic actors.
The commercial exchange of goods and services between buyers and sellers.
The exchange of capital, goods, and services across international borders or territories.
The ability of an economic actor to produce a specific good or service at a lower opportunity cost than a trading partner.
The process by which individuals, firms, or nations concentrate their productive efforts on a limited variety of activities.
The separation of a work process into a number of tasks, with each task performed by a separate person or group.
The costs incurred in the process of making an economic exchange, including search, negotiation, and enforcement costs.
Economic agents who facilitate trade by bringing buyers and sellers together, helping reduce transaction costs.
The simultaneous purchase and sale of an asset in different markets to profit from price discrepancies.
The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at various prices during a given period.
The specific amount of a good or service that buyers are willing and able to purchase at a single, specific price point.
The economic principle stating that, ceteris paribus, as the price of a good increases, quantity demanded decreases.
A graphical representation of the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded for a given period of time.
The subjective individual tastes, as measured by utility, that dictate consumer purchasing choices across various bundles of goods.
A measure of how responsive the quantity demanded of a good is to a change in its price.
A condition in which a percentage change in price leads to an exact equal and opposite percentage change in quantity demanded.
A theoretical situation where consumers will buy a fixed quantity of a good regardless of its price.
Goods or services that can be used in place of one another, where a price increase in one leads to increased demand for the other.
Products typically consumed together, such that a decrease in the price of one leads to an increase in demand for the other.
Goods for which demand decreases as consumer income rises.
Goods for which demand increases as consumer income rises.
The sacrifices made to obtain a good or service that are not expressed in financial terms, such as time, effort, or discomfort.
The total amount of a specific good or service that is available to consumers at various prices.
A graphical representation showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied.
A measure of how much the quantity supplied of a good responds to a change in its price.
The process of combining various material and immaterial inputs in order to make something for consumption.
A curve depicting all maximum output possibilities for two goods, given a set of inputs and technology, demonstrating trade-offs and opportunity cost.
The expenses a business incurs to produce and deliver goods or services to consumers.
The cost of the next best alternative given up in order to produce one more unit of a good.
The total cost of production divided by the number of units produced.
The change in total production cost that comes from making or producing one additional unit.
A cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered, which should rationally not affect future economic decisions.
The process of assigning and managing available assets in a manner that best meets the strategic goals or consumer demands.
Any structure or arrangement that allows buyers and sellers to exchange any type of goods, services, and information.
The continuous unfolding of interactions among buyers, sellers, and entrepreneurs resolving inefficiencies and aligning supply with demand.
The process by which the price of a good adjusts so that the quantity supplied precisely equals the quantity demanded.
The specific price at which the quantity demanded of a good exactly matches the quantity supplied.
The state where economic forces such as supply and demand are balanced, stabilizing the price.
Prices established by the unrestricted interaction of supply and demand without government intervention.
An economic system in which prices are determined by market forces, conveying essential information for resource allocation.
Messages sent to consumers and producers via the changing of relative prices, guiding decisions on consumption and production.
A government-imposed legal limit on how high a price is allowed to be charged for a product.
A government-imposed legal limit on how low a price can be charged for a product.
Governmental restrictions on the prices that can be charged for goods and services in a market.
A macroeconomic condition wherein the general price level in an economy does not change significantly over time.
The practice of sharply raising prices on essential goods to a level considered unfair, typically during a demand shock or emergency.
A pricing strategy where identical or largely similar goods or services are sold at different prices by the same provider in different markets.
A system of surcharging users of public goods or services that are subject to congestion during periods of peak demand.
The illegal or unethical act of setting prices low in an attempt to eliminate competition.
A pricing strategy where a fixed percentage is added on top of the cost to produce one unit of a product.
The rivalry among sellers trying to achieve such goals as increasing profits, market share, and sales volume.
The dynamic view of competition as an ongoing process of entrepreneurial discovery rather than a static end-state.
An association of manufacturers or suppliers with the purpose of maintaining prices at a high level and restricting competition.
The artificial limitation of output by a dominant firm or group of firms to raise prices and secure higher profits.
Agreements or terms between firms at different levels of the production and distribution chain restricting conditions under which firms may purchase or sell.
The mechanism by which markets reveal previously unknown information about consumer preferences, resource scarcity, and production methods.
The activity of setting up a business, undertaking risks, and alertly discovering unexploited profit opportunities in the market.
The financial gain achieved when the amount of revenue gained from a business activity exceeds the expenses, costs, and taxes.
The difference between total revenue and total costs, where total costs include both explicit and implicit (opportunity) costs.
A company's total earnings, calculated according to generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), subtracting explicitly incurred costs from revenue.
The profit remaining after all costs of capital have been deducted from operating profit.
The financial outcome that occurs when a business's total expenses exceed its total revenues.
The economic agent who possesses the right to receive whatever profits remain after all other legitimate claims on an enterprise's revenues have been met.
A condition involving outcomes for which probabilities cannot be accurately calculated or foreseen.
A situation where the probability of a specific undesired outcome can be estimated using statistical methods.
The practical implementation of ideas that result in the introduction of new goods or services or improvement in offering goods or services.
The purchase or sale of an asset with the hope of benefiting from future price movements, thus providing liquidity and assuming risk.
A central financial exchange where people can trade standardized futures contracts.
An investment strategy executed to offset or reduce the risk of adverse price movements in an asset.
The system or group of people governing an organized community, possessing a monopoly on the legitimate use of coercive force.
The broad welfare or well-being of the general public, often invoked as the rationale for government intervention.
Goods that are both non-excludable and non-rivalrous, meaning individuals cannot be effectively excluded from use and use by one does not reduce availability.
A market failure that occurs when those who benefit from resources, public goods, or common pool resources do not pay for them.
Costs or benefits incurred or received by a third party who has no control over the factors that created the cost or benefit.
A benefit that is enjoyed by a third-party as a result of an economic transaction.
A cost that is suffered by a third party as a result of an economic transaction.
The specific economic burdens placed on uninvolved third parties due to negative externalities.
A strategic discussion that aims to resolve an issue or reach an agreement in a mutually acceptable way.
The legal process by which an arbiter or judge reviews evidence and argumentation to enforce property rights or contracts.
Rules or directives made and maintained by an authority that control the way a business can operate.
The framework of legal institutions and enforcement mechanisms that maintain societal stability and secure property rights.
The transfer of income and wealth from some individuals to others through social mechanisms such as taxation and welfare.
Action taken together by a group of people whose goal is to enhance their status or achieve a common objective.
A standard example of a game analyzed in game theory that shows why two completely rational individuals might not cooperate, even if it appears in their best interests to do so.
Money that an individual or business receives in exchange for providing labor, producing a good or service, or investing capital.
How a nation’s total GDP is distributed amongst its population.
The economic value of a worker's experience and skills, including education, training, and health.
The flow of usable energy, time, or skill from labor, land, or capital equipment into the production process.
The amount of physical, mental, and social effort used to produce goods and services in an economy.
Demand for a factor of production or intermediate good that occurs as a result of the demand for another intermediate or final good.
A payment usually of money for labor or services usually according to contract and on an hourly, daily, or piecework basis.
Any payment to an owner or factor of production in excess of the costs needed to bring that factor into production.
The charge for the privilege of borrowing money, typically expressed as annual percentage rate (APR).
The lowest remuneration that employers can legally pay their employees.
A situation where individuals who are employable and seeking a job are unable to find work.
A state or condition in which a person or community lacks the financial resources and essentials for a minimum standard of living.
The unequal distribution of income and opportunity between different groups in society.
The ability of an individual, family, or some other group to improve (or lower) their economic status—usually measured in income.
Any item or verifiable record that is generally accepted as payment for goods and services and repayment of debts.
A government-issued currency that is not backed by a physical commodity, such as gold or silver, but rather by the government that issued it.
A negotiable promissory note issued by a bank and payable to the bearer on demand.
A generally accepted form of money, including coins and paper notes, which is issued by a government and circulated within an economy.
Funds deposited in a bank that can be withdrawn at any time by presenting a check.
The total volume of money held by the public at a particular point in time in an economy.
The state where the quantity of money supplied by the central bank and the banking system equals the quantity of money demanded by the public.
The process by which the monetary authority of a country controls the supply of money, often targeting an inflation rate or interest rate.
The rate of increase in prices over a given period of time, corresponding to a decline in the purchasing power of money.
A general decline in prices for goods and services, typically associated with a contraction in the supply of money and credit.
A temporary slowing of the pace of price inflation, where the inflation rate is still positive but decreasing.
Very high and typically accelerating inflation, rapidly eroding the real value of the local currency.
An economic condition characterized by slow growth and high unemployment (stagnation) accompanied by rising prices (inflation).
The difference between the face value of money, such as a coin or paper money, and the cost to produce it, forming revenue for the government.
The buying and selling of government securities in the open market in order to expand or contract the amount of money in the banking system.
The interest rate charged to commercial banks and other depository institutions on loans they receive from their regional central bank's lending facility.
A central bank regulation that sets the minimum amount of reserves that must be held by a commercial bank.
The process by which the banking system creates multiple times more deposits and money out of fractional reserve lending.
An unconventional monetary policy in which a central bank purchases long-term securities from the open market to increase the money supply and encourage lending and investment.

The trust which allows one party to provide money or resources to another party wherein the second party does not reimburse the first party immediately but promises either to repay or return those resources later.
The portion of income not spent on current expenditures, setting aside funds for future use or investment.
The purchase of goods that are not consumed today but are used in the future to create wealth.
An amount of money borrowed by one party from another, subject to a repayment arrangement, usually involving interest.
The total amount of money that a country's government has borrowed by various means.
The amount by which a government's expenditures exceed its revenues during a particular period, typically a year.
The use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy.
The amount charged, expressed as a percentage of principal, by a lender to a borrower for the use of assets.
The interest rate before taking inflation into account.
An interest rate that has been adjusted to remove the effects of inflation to reflect the real cost of funds to the borrower and the real yield to the lender.
A period of rapid economic expansion fueled by excessive credit creation that ultimately cannot be maintained and leads to a bust.
A situation in which one party gets involved in a risky event knowing that it is protected against the risk and the other party will incur the cost.
The total monetary or market value of all the finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
An estimate of total value of all the final products and services turned out in a given period by the means of production owned by a country's residents.
The economy-wide movements in macroeconomic variables such as total output, employment, and the general price level.
An increase in the production of economic goods and services, compared from one period of time to another.
A significant decline in general economic activity in a designated region typically recognized after two consecutive quarters of economic decline.
The natural fluctuation of the economy between periods of expansion (growth) and contraction (recession).
The total value of a country's final output of all new goods and services produced in one year.
The difference between the price of a product or service and the cost of producing it.
The statistical tracking and evaluation of the aggregate economy's health, often through metrics like GDP, inflation, and unemployment.
The process by which the economic well-being and quality of life of a nation, region, local community, or an individual are improved according to targeted goals.
The increasing interaction of people through the growth of the international flow of money, ideas, and culture.
Flows of capital from one nation to another in exchange for significant ownership stakes in domestic companies or other domestic assets.
Money, food, or other resources given or lent by one country to another, typically for developmental or humanitarian purposes.
The fundamental right of every human to control his or her own labor and property without government coercion or constraint.
An economic system in which the production of goods and services is based principally on knowledge-intensive activities.
The process of building up the capital stock of a country through investment in physical and human capital.
The process of acquiring and increasing the number of persons who have the skills, education and experience which are critical for the economic growth of the country.
The business practice of hiring a party outside a company to perform services or create goods that were traditionally performed in-house.
A set of measures, both economic and humanitarian, that are intended to permanently lift people out of poverty.
An analytical approach to understanding human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.
The methodological practice of properly structuring inquiries to yield accurate economic insights and avoid fallacies.
Outcomes of a purposeful action that are not intended or foreseen, frequently emphasized in the economic analysis of policy interventions.
The mental habit of recognizing that every decision requires sacrificing the next best alternative.
The systematic approach of comparing the expected costs and benefits of an action to determine its net value.
The way in which decentralized markets align the disparate plans and actions of buyers and sellers without central direction.
The theory that the knowledge required to efficiently allocate resources is dispersed among individuals and cannot be successfully aggregated by a central planner.
Decisions and behaviors directed toward achieving a specific end while utilizing the minimum possible amount of scarce resources.
The study of how formal and informal rules, laws, and customs shape human behavior and economic outcomes.
The examination of the rewards and penalties within a system to predict how individuals will behave.
The assessment of real-world alternative institutional arrangements rather than comparing real-world imperfections to an ideal theoretical standard.
